Khondker Mahbubul Hossain with ABM Siddiqur Rahman Khan, Mamun Chowdhury, Affan Ahmed Siddique and Humayun Kabir Monzu, Advocates-For Convict-Appellant No. 2.

parties:
Muhibur Rahman Manik and another ----- Convict-Appellants
vs. 
State ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J: Abul Kalam Babul and Arif Haider suffered death following explosion of explosive substances on 15-3-1999. Abu Lyes Chowdhury was, also, a prey of explosion. Arena of explosion is a two-storied building at 200, Udaychal, Mandalibagh, Hospital Road, Chatak Pourashava. Muhibur Rahman Manik, a sitting Member of Parliament on the date of incident, was depicted as owner of occurrence two-storied building.

2. In respect of explosion of bomb, Muhibur Rahman Manik on 16-3-1999 bestowed a first information report (Exhibit 19) with Chatak Police Station. Date of occurrence was stated to be on 15-3-1999 at 15.43 hours. First information report led to registration of Chatak Police Station Case No. 8(3)99.

3. Seizure of incriminating articles had been caused. Nine (9) items of articles had been seized on 16-3-1999 and seizure list had been prepared. Witnesses to seizure put their signature on seizure list. Original copy of seizure list is Exhibit 3 and photocopy of the said seizure list is Exhibit 6. One (1) item of article had been seized on 19-5-1999. Seizure list had been prepared. Witnesses to seizure put their signatures. Seizure list dated 19-5-1999 is Exhibit 7. Autopsy on cadavers of deceased Abul Kalam Babul and Arif Haider had been performed by PW 25. During performance of Post Mortem on corpse of Arif Haider he could not be identified but thereafter, he was identified as Arif Haider.

4. Abdus Salam, the then Officer-in-Charge of Chatak Police Station, on 26-3-1999 at 16:05 hours as informant laid second information report with Chatak Police Station. In second information report date of occurrence was stated to be 15-3-1999 at 15:40 hours and, also, 24-3-1999 at 8-00 hours-14-30 hours. Abu Lyes Choudhury and Gopal had been brought under indictment of offence punishable under sections 3, 4 and 6 of Explosive Substances Act, 1908. Second information report was registered as Chatak Police Station Case No. 13(3) 1999.

5. Police on strength of second information report placed Police Report in the form of charge-sheet against Muhibur Rahman Manik, Abu Lyes Choudhury, Biplob Bhuiyan, Belal Ahmed, Zakaria Chowdhury and Gopal Chandra Das under sections 3, 4 and 6 of Explosive Substances Act.

6. The above six (6) accused persons had been booked for trial before Druto Bichar Tribunal, Sylhet in Druto Bichar (Explosive Sub-stance) Case No. 4 of 2003 under charge of sections 3, 4 and 6 of Explosive Substances Act Gopal Chandra Das, having been in ascendance, was tried in absentia.

7. Prosecution case projected in second information report dated 26-3-1999 and unfurled during trial is as hereunder :

On 15-3-1999 there was an explosion from explosive substances in one of the rooms of first floor of Muhibur Rahman Manik's two-storied building. Two persons, namely Abul Kalam Babul and Arif Haider, died and Abu Lyes Choudhury was seriously injured following the explosion. Surroundings of occurrence room collapsed and hole had peen created in the floor of the room. Incriminating articles alleged to have been used for manufacturing bombs/cocktails were seized and first floor of the said building was closed down and since 16-3-1999 to 26-3-1999 the whole premises had been under control of police. Persons named in first information report and persons breathed their last at the scene of occurrence were very much intimate to Muhibur Rahman Manik. Explosion took place inadvertently while deceased persons were manufacturing, cocktails by explosive materials.

8. Prosecution, in proof of guilt of accused persons, put on witness box thirtysix (36) witnesses.

9. Out of 36 witnesses, PW 1 is Informant. PWs 2, 3, 13, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 32, 33, 34, 35 and 36 are official witnesses. Rest 22 witnesses are public witnesses. Of public witnesses PWs 9, 12, 18, 19 and 24 had been tendered from prosecution and cross-examination had been declined from defence. PWs 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15 17, 20, 21, 22, 23, 30 and 31 had been declared hostile by prosecution and they did not support prosecution version.

10. Defence adopted from side of accused Muhibur Rahman Manik are:

a. He is absolutely innocent and he had no complicity in the crime. He was quite in darkness about the explosion incident. He had been falsely implicated in the case.

b. He has become a victim of political rivalry and conspiracy and he has been involved in the case just to spoil his political career.

c. Candidate supported by him in the last Chatak Pourashava Election won election and his political enemies got infuriated over their defeat in Chatak Pourashava Election. Through unknown miscreants they blasted bombs in the room of the building. He was in Dhaka on the incident day.

11. Defence adopted by accused Abu Lyes Choudhury is:

a. He on 15-3-1999 at 9-00 AM went to his work place i.e. shop, and at 03-15 PM he along with Muzibur Rahman on a rickshaw reached the incident building and on his way to his room there had been an explosion and he suffered injuries on different parts of his body.

b. He was not aware how and by whom explosion episode took place.

12. Defence adopted by other accused persons was their innocence and false implication in the case.

13. On conclusion of trial, accused per-sons were examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and during their examination they insisted on their innocence and false and malafide implication in the case.

14. Druto Bichar Tribunal found accused Muhibur Rahman Manik guilty of offence punishable under section 6 of Explosive Sub-stances Act and convicted him there under. Following conviction he was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for ten (10) years. He was, also, slapped with a fine of Taka 5,000 and to suffer further rigorous imprisonment for six (6) months in default of payment of fine. Druto Bichar Tribunal found accused Abu Lyes Choudhury and Gopal Chandra Das (in ascendance) guilty of offence of section 4 of the Act of 1908 and convicted them thereunder. Consequential sentence was rigorous imprisonment for ten (10) years and a fine of Taka 5,000 each and further rigorous imprisonment for six (6) months in default of payment of fine. Druto Bichar Tribunal found accused Md Zakaria Chowdhury, Billal Ahmed and Md Biplob Bhuiyan not guilty of the charge staged against them and pronounced a verdict of acquittal upon them. Judgment had been handed down on 9-10-2004.

15. Convict Muhibur Rahman Manik and Abu Lyes Choudhury could not accept the verdict of conviction and sentence awarded upon them and they sought setting aside those on presentation of a Petition of Appeal before this Court under section 14 of Druto Bichar Tribunal Act of 2002. Convicts shall be referred to hereinafter as convict-appellants.

16. Sustainability of conviction and sentence awarded upon convict-appellants has been bombarded pressing into service a good number of contentions. Of those, core contentions are catalogued hereunder:

i. Prosecution signally failed to bring home charge against the convict-appellants by any legal evidence what sever.

ii. It is in the evidence of Informant PW 1 that explosion of explosive substances occurred in Room No.3 of first floor of Muhibur Rahman Manik MP's residence. Sketch map No.2 (Exhibit 15) and Index (Exhibit 17) of sketch map No 2 (Exhibit 15) is indicative of fact that explosion did not take place in the room of convict appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik nor in the room of convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury and convict-appellants cannot be connected with commission of offence punishable under sections 6 and 4 respectively of the Explosive Substances Act.

iii. Evidence of PW 5 manifests that incriminating articles had been brought from outside and evidence of PW 5 destroyed the whole prosecution case that incriminating articles i.e. materials for preparation of bombs and cocktails, had been found and re-covered from occurrence building.

iv. PW 6, a seizure list witness though laid bare in his evidence that he saw cock-tails in scattered condition when he approached on occurrence building on the following day of the incident. PW 6 was examined by police under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure after a period of 52 days and his evidence in Court is to be left out of consideration.

v. Charge framed against convict-appellants are seriously defective.

vi. Convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik laid first information report with Chatak Police Station on 16-3-1999 and that report was earliest report in point of time supplied to Police Station in respect of a cognizable offence but prosecution case rested on the basis of second information report laid by information PW 1 and prosecution case built up on second information report suffers from gross illegality and infirmity and conviction and sentence awarded upon convict-appellants cannot be sustained in law.

Kashem alias Md Abul Kashem vs State 47 DLR 438, Mohammad Usman Mohammad Hussain Maniyar and another vs State of Maharashtra AIR 1981 SC 1062, Bimal Pershad Jain vs Emperor, AIR 1934 Lahore 583, The State of Bihar vs Amir Hasan, AIR (38) 1951 Patna 638, Abdul Rahim vs The King, AIR (38) 1951 Patna 319 and Pramatha Nath Talukder and Surendra Mohan Basu vs Saroj Ranjan Sarkar AIR 1962 SC 876 have been referred to in support of the contentions advanced.

17. Rejoinder to above contentions has been offered from the side of State-respondent in advancing counter-contentions which are:

i. Convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik provided premises to deceased persons and convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury and, as such, he is liable to be punished under section 6 of Explosive Substances Act.

ii. Circumstantial evidence is so insurmountable that no other inference other than the guilt of the convict-appellants can be drawn and convict-appellants had been rightly convicted and sentenced by Druto Bichar Tribunal.

iii. Charges had been composed in accordance with law against convict-appellants and no illegality and defect occurred in framing charge against convict-appellants.

iv. Second information report is very much permissible in law when no of-fence had been disclosed in first information report and names of offenders had not been, also, noted in first information report and no exception can be taken to the verdict of conviction and sentence awarded upon convict-appellants on the basis of second information report.

In support of the contentions, reliance has been put upon Lutfor Rahman alias Arju and another vs State 51 DLR (AD) 120, Amritalal Hazra and others vs Emperor AIR 1916 Calcutta 188, Abdul Rahman vs State PLD 1975 SC 275 and State vs Khondker Zillul Bari and Zahirul Alam and another 57 DLR (AD) 129.

18. On Judicial Decision, it can profitably be observed that a Judicial decision is only an authority for what it actually decides. It cannot be quoted for a proposition that may seem to follow from it. Every judgment must be read applicable to the particular facts proved or assumed to be proved. Generality of expression that may be found cannot be intended to be exposition of whole law but must he regarded as governed or qualified by particular facts of the case in which such expression occurs. It is neither desirable nor permissible to pick up a word or sentence from the Judgment divorced from the context of the question under consideration and to treat it to be complete law declared by Court.

19. In the wake of view contentions advanced from the Bar, the points which outlast for determination are:

i. How far the prosecution succeeded in driving home the charge to the doors of convict-appellants beyond any speck of doubt.

ii. Whether the verdict of conviction and sentence awarded upon convict-appellants can be sustained in law, evidences, materials on record, fact and circumstances of the case and, also, in safe dispensation of Criminal Justice

and

iii. Whether convict-appellants can be liberated of the charge staged against them on bestowing a ruling of acquittal on finding them not guilty of the charge.

20. Fundamental and basic principles in the Administration of Criminal Law and Justice Delivery System is the innocence of alleged accused and till charges are proved beyond shadow of doubt on the basis of clear, cogent, credible and unimpeachable evidence, question of indicting or punishing an accused does not arise. Right of accused to obtain benefit of reasonable doubt is the necessary outcome and counterpart of prosecution's undeniable duty to establish its case beyond reasonable doubt. Prosecution version is required to be judged taking into account overall fact and circumstance of the case with a practical, pragmatic and reasonable approach in appreciation of evidence let in to drive home guilt of accused person. Mental distance between "may be true" and "must be true" and distinction between "conjecture" and "sure conclusions" are to be gathered on the touchstone of dispassionate Judicial scrutiny based upon a complete and comprehensive appreciation of features of the case as well as quality and credibility of evidence and materials brought on record.

21. The expression "Reasonable Doubt" is incapable of definition. Plain meaning of "Doubt" is uncertainty of mind, the absence of a settled opinion or conviction, the attitude towards acceptance of a belief in proposition, theory or statement.

A definition often quoted or followed is that given by Chief Justice Shaw in the Webster case which is as hereunder:

It is not mere possible doubt, because everything relating to human affairs and depending upon moral evidence is open to some possible or imaginary doubt. It is that state of case, which after the entire comparison and consideration of all the evidences leave the mind of the jurors in that consideration that they cannot say they feel an abiding conviction to a moral certainty of the truth of the charge.

22. On legal burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the oft-quoted observation of Lord Sankey LC in Wilmington vs Director of Public Prosecutions (1935) AC 1462 may be noticed which are couched in the following language:

"If at the end of and on the whole of the case there is a reasonable doubt created by the evidence given by either the prosecution or the prisoner, as to whether the prisoner killed the deceased with a malicious intention, the prosecution has not made out the case and the prisoner is entitled to an acquittal".

23. In the yardstick of above stated principles, the points formulated are now approached and answered.

24. In getting closer to the points, meticulous assessment of fact and circumstances of the case, intensive appraisal of rightful evidences, a legal survey of provision of law and legal aspects touching the case are, also, required to be taken stock of.

25. Information about the incident which is offered under sub-section 1 of section 154 of the Code and carried to police station at the earliest opportunity of the incident is known as first information report, though, this term is not used in the Code. First information report marks the commencement of investigation which ends up with the formation of opinion under section 169 or 170, as the case may be, and forwarding of a Police Report under section 173 of the Code. It is quite possible, and it happens not infrequently, that more information than one are given to a Police Officer-in-Charge of a Police Station in respect of the, same incident involving one or more cognizable offences. In such a case, Police Officer did not enter every one of them in the Diary and this is implied in section 154 of the Code. Information first entered into Police Station Diary kept for this purpose and by a police officer, incharge of a police station, is first information report postulated in section 154 of the Code. All other information made orally or in writing after commencement of investigation into the cognizable offence disclosed from facts encompassed in first information report and entered in Police Station Diary by Police Officer or such other cognizable offence as may come to his notice during investigation shall be statements falling under section 162 of the Code. No such information/statement can properly be treated as a first information report and entered in police station diary again, as it would be, in effect, a second information report and the same cannot be in conformity with the scheme of the Code itself.

26. The scheme of the Code is, that an Officer-in-charge of a police station has to commence investigation as provided in section 156 or 157 of the Code on the basis of entry of first information report on coming to know of commission of a cognizable offence. On completion of investigation and on the basis of evidence collected, he has to form an opinion under section 169 or 170 of the Code, as the case may be, and forward his Report to Magistrate concerned under section 173(2) of the Code. However, even after filing such a report, if he comes into possession of further information or material, he need not register a fresh first information report; he is empowered to make further investigation, normally with the leave of the Court, and where during further investigation he collects further evidence, oral or documentary, he is obliged to forward the same, with one or more further reports. This is the import of section 173 of the Code.

27. In Muslimuddin and others vs State, 1987 BLD AD 1= 38 DLR (AD) 311 the legal debate which fell for determination was which of the information would be the first information report within the meaning of section 154 of the Code. It has been held in paragraph No. 52 of the Judgment that in point of time information carried to the police by "some body" is first information report within the meaning of section 154 of the Code and all subsequent information fall within the purview of section 161 of the CrPC.

28. In Zilu Mia and others vs State 1988 BLD 418 a Division Bench of the High Court Division in taking into account principles enunciated in Mani Mohan Ghose vs The King Emperor 35 CWN 623 and Ghulam Kadir vs Crown PLD 1950 Baghdadul Jadid 51 held that the information first received by the police where-upon investigation was started and the appellants were arrested is the first information report and that is admissible but the information subsequently recorded at 11-00 PM in the night of occurrence is not admissible in evidence and, therefore, it cannot be taken into consideration.

29. In Ali Sher vs State PLD 1966 (WP) 368 it has been laid down that a first information report after the police investigation has started being a statement of a person before the police, is not admissible in evidence and cannot be taken into consideration.

30. The legal controversy, also, came up for consideration before Supreme Court of India in TT Antony vs State of Kerala and others, with Damodarau P and others vs State of Kerala and others and State of Kerala and others vs Revada Chandrasekhar and others, 2001 SCC (Cri) 1048 = AIR 2001 SC 2637. In the said case in regard to an occurrence in the vicinity of Kuthuparamba Police Station, Superintendent of Police registered Crime No. 354 of 1994 on the strength of a first information report. A second information report under section 154 of the Code had been registered on the basis of the letter of the Director General of Police as Crime No. 268 of 1997 of Kuthuparamba Police Station. The Supreme Court of India took into stock the scheme of provisions of sections 154, 155, 156, 157, 162, 169, 170 and 173 of the Code and came to hold—

Under the scheme of provisions of sections 154, 155, 156, 157, 162, 169, 170 and 173 of the CrPC only the earliest or the first information report in regard to the commission of cognizable offence satisfies the requirements of section 154 of the Code. Thus, there can be no second first information report and consequently there can be no fresh investigation on receipt of every subsequent information in respect of the same cognisable offence or the same occurrence or incident giving rise to one or more cognisable offences on receipt of information about a cognisable offence or an incident giving rise to cognisable offence or offences and or entering the first information report in the station house diary, the officer-in-charge of a police station has to investigate not merely the cognisable offence reported in the first information report but, also other connected offences found to have been committed in the course of the same transaction or the same occurrence and file one or more reports as provided in section 173 of the Code.

The Supreme Court of India, thus, held that registration of second information report under section 154 of the CrPC on the basis of a letter of Director General of Police as Crime No. 268 of 1997 of Kuthuparamba Police Station is not valid and consequently, investigation made pursuant thereof is of no legal consequence. Recording the above observation and views, the Supreme Court of India qua-shed the second information report laid under section 154 of the Code lodged in respect of an incident on which there had been an earlier first information report.

31. Incident took place on 15-3-1999. First information report (Exhibit 19) was presented by convict-appellant Mohibur Rahman Manik and that first information report is earliest in point of time. In the said first information report incident of explosion of bomb/cocktail had been very much stated i.e. a cognisable offence has been disclosed. The said first information report was registered as Chatak Police Station Case No. 8(3) 1999. It emerged from evidence of Informant PW 1 that he himself took up investigation of the case and he performed some investigation and thereafter, on the order of Higher Authority, transferred the case to Criminal Investigation Department and Criminal Investigation Department submitted Final Report and, against that, a petition (Narajee) arose and that Narajee Petition stood rejected on 10-11-1999. During the lifetime of first information report second information report had been laid by informant PW 1, the then Officer-in-charge of Chatak Police Station, which led to registration of Chatak Police Station Case No. 13(4) 1999. second information report was laid after a period of 11 days of the incident and 10 days of the lodgment of first information report. Fate of first information report dated 16-3-1999 (Exhibit 19) was not known and no Police Report either in the form of Charge Sheet or Final Report appeared to have been laid. PW 36 (Investigating Officer), although made disclosure in his evidence that Final Report had been submitted in that case and, also, it came out from his mouth that he took up investigation of the case and on the order of Superior Authority the case record was transmitted to the Criminal Investigation Department and the said Department on investigation submitted Final Report and Protest Petition (Naraji) had been rejected but no paper, no document are on record in support of the testimony of PW 1 that Final Report had been submitted in Chatak Police Station Case No. 8(3)99. No paper had been produced in the case demonstrating that Metropolitan Magistrate accepted Final Report or that Protest Petition presented by Informant Muhibur Rahman Manik stood rejected. In the absence of any paper and document in respect of alleged submission of Final Report in Chatak Police Station Case No. 8(3) 99, it is difficult to accept the version of PW 1 that Final Report had been submitted in Chatak Police Station Case No. 8(3) 1999.

<u>32. In second information report no explanation had been offered in respect of lodgment of the same in the face of existence of first information report. In charge sheet dated 28-7-1999 there is, also, no reference that Police Report in the form of Final Report had been submitted in Chatak Police Station Case No. 8(3)99.</u>

<u>33. Presentation of a second information report by Informant PW 1 after a period of 11 days of the explosion incident and about 10 days of the lodgment of first information report by convict appellant Mohibur Rahman Manik and using of incriminating articles seized in Chatak Police Station Case No. 8(3)-1999 which originated from first information report in the subsequent Chatak Police Station Case No. 13(3)1999 which sprouted up from second information report is a very much disturbing phenomena striking at the root of prosecution case. Report dated 26-3-1999 cannot be said to be first information report falling within the purview of section 154 of the Code and the said report treated as first information report was manifestly a second information report and the text comprised in second information report was statement falling under section 162 of the Code. Under the law there could not be any second information report and there could not be any investigation on the strength of second information report. Second information report was not at all valid and legal. Investigation performed on the basis of second information report and submission of charge-sheet and commencement of trial pursuant to charge sheet on second first information report was of no legal consequence and recording of conviction for offence of sections 4 and 6 of Explosive Substances Act and consequential sentence prized upon convict-appellant are absolutely illegal and demonstratively infirm. Druto Bichar Tribunal did not at all take into account this facet of prosecution case and committed substantial error in the decision in awarding conviction and sentence upon convict-appellants and judgment of conviction and sentence deserves to be quashed.</u>

34. Case laws reckoned from the State-respondent now may be adverted to. In Amritalal Hazra vs Emperor (Supra) three principles had been propounded which are:

i. In charge of criminal conspiracy for getting in possession of explosives the explosive substance must be specified.

ii. In order to justify the inference of guilt the exculpatory facts must be incompatible with the innocence of the accused and incapable of explanation upon any other reasonable hypothesis than that of truth and

iii. In a charge under section 4(b) of The Explosive Substances Act, 1908 possession, to be punishable, must also be possession with knowledge and assent.

We are in respectful agreement with the principles enunciated in the Judicial Pronouncement.

35. In Abdul Rahman vs State (Supra) in respect of an unwitnessed occurrence, one Taslim Ahmed (DW 1) had offered earliest information which was recorded as "Roznamcha". Police Officer who was examined as DW 2 did not record the information as first information report under section 154 of the Code as because the information was vague and particulars had not been given. Subsequently, a report had been lodged. Md Afzal Choudhury held that since the Report laid by DW 2 did not disclose the name of the assailant or otherwise give counter-version, it could not discredit the FIR recorded shortly after. The fact and circumstances of the case got no bearing in the fact and circumstances of the case in hand.

36. In The State vs Khandker Zillul Bari, Zahirul Alam Kamal and another (Supra) daughter-in-law of Khalilur Rahman was found dead in the house of Khalilur Rahman. On getting information over telephone that the daughter-in-law of Khalilur Rahman was dead in the house he went to the house and then he proceeded towards hospital. In hospital police officer found some members of the house of Khalilur Rahman and asked them to lodge first information report with Police Station and first information report was then laid by Nasiruddin Jamal. Investigation of the case was taken over by CID and on investigation it came to light that the residents of the house along with other accused persons were responsible for causing murder of the daughter-in-law of Khalilur Rahman. CID officer then submitted Final Report in respect of first information report filed by Nasiruddin Jamal and there-after, a suo moto first information report was lodged and on investigation he submitted charge sheet against Khandker Zillul Bari and some others. In the case in hand, second information report was lodged during the lifetime of first information report. Fact and circumstances of this case is, also, quite distinguishable in the fact and circumstances of the case in our hand. State-respondent cannot derive any benefit from the two Judicial authorities relied upon by it.

37. Convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik and convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury had been condemned for offence punishable under sections 6 and 4 respectively of Explosive Substances Act. Respective case of each of the convict-appellants shall now be considered.

38. Case of convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik is taken up first.

39. Muhibur Rahman Manik stood convicted for offence of section 6 of the Act of 1908.

40. Section 6 runs thus:

Punishment of abettors. Any person who by the supply of or solicitation for money, the providing of premises, the supply of materials, or in any manner whatsoever, procures, counsels, aids, abets, or is accessory to, the commission of any offence under this Act shall be punished with the punishment provided for the offence.

41. Section 6 enshrines that a person who by supply of or solicitation for money, providing of premises, supply of materials, or in any manner procures, counsels, aids, abets, or is accessory to, the commission of any offence, shall be punished under the section.

42. The debate now comes whether convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik committed offence of section 6 of the Act of 1908 by supply of or solicitation of money, providing premises, supplying of materials, procured, counseled, aided, abetted or was accessory to the commission of offence of section 6 of The Act of 1908.

<u>43. In second information report, convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik was not brought within the dragnet of any offence whatsoever, though it was laid after a period of 11 days of explosion incident. Convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik was admittedly in Dhaka and, as such, he was not in occurrence building when explosion came about. Druto Bichar Tribunal, also, positively held that at the time of explosion of bomb accused Muhibur Rahman Manik had been in Dhaka and from his direct possession no explosive substances had been recovered. There had been no accusation, nor an iota of evidence that bombs and cocktails were being manufactured m bedroom of convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik. There is no scintilla of evidence that convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik procured, counseled, aided or abetted the commission of offence nor there is any evidence that convict-appellant either supplied money or solicited for money or provided the premises or supplied materials for commission of any offence under Explosive Substances Act of 1908. There is nothing suggesting, that he was an accessory to an offence either of sections 3, 4(a) and 4(b) and 5 of the Act of 1908.</u>

<u>44. Optimistic case of prosecution programmed in the second information report is that explosion took place in room No. 3 of first floor building which was owned and possessed by convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik. Exhibit 14 is sketch map No. I prepared on 26-3-1999. In Exhibit 14 'R' "is marked as place of occurrence building". There is no specification of room No.3 within 'R' shown in sketch map No. 1. Exhibit 16 is Index of sketch map No.1 (Exhibit 14) wherein, also, room No.3 of incident building had not been shown and only 'R' had been shown as place of occurrence "two storied building": R ঘটনাস্থল দ্বিতল ভবন. Exhibit 15 is sketch map No. 2 prepared on 26-3-1999. In the said sketch map A, P, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N, O, had been noted. Exhibit 17 is Index of sketch map No. 2. In Index (Exhibit 17) "B" had been shown as the room wherein MP Shaheb (Muhibur Rahman Manik) used to reside. "C" has been shown as place of occurrence where there had been explosion and Belal, cousin brother of MP Shaheb had been stated to have resided there. "D" had been shown as room of Abu Lyes Choudhury wherein he was stated to have resided and from where pot of Elite Paint containing "Cocktails" and "Ramdao" and "0.22 Rimball" and "Empty" were said to have been recovered. From the above sketch map and index it became manifestly clear that there had been no explosion in the room of convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik wherein convict-appellant was stated to have stayed which was spotted as "B" in Index Map and, also, in room of convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury which was fixed as "D" in Index and explosion allegedly took place in room of accused Belal which was spotted as "C" in Index Map. Sketch map No. 2 (Exhibit 15), Index of sketch map No. 1 (Exhibit 16) and Index of sketch map. No. 2 (Exhibit 17) pulverized the edifice of prosecution case that explosion took place in the room of convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik. Druto Bichar Tribunal failed to consider Exhibit 15 and Exhibit 17 and committed a substantial error in awarding conviction and sentence upon convict-appellants on finding them guilty of offence under sections 4 and 6 of Explosive Substan</u>ces Act.

45. It is in the evidence of Informant PW 1 that the elder brothers of Muhibur Rahman Manik, Muzibor Rahman and Mustafizur Rahman, resided in the same building and his another brother stayed in England. From the evidence of Informant PW 1 the point had been crystallized that convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik is not the absolute owner of the occurrence building and the occurrence building is also, owned and possessed by his other three full brothers. Endeavour mounted from the side of prosecution to show convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik as the absolute owner of occurrence building stood broken to smithereens.

46. PW 5, the seizure list witness blurted out in his evidence that he did not find any-thing except dead bodies. It is, also, his evidence that he found five bags but he did not see what had been in the bag and the contents of the seizure list had not been placed to him and he said that his signature appeared in the photocopy of the seizure list. It is his lip evidence that war of words took place between Dr Abdul Gani and police and Dr. Gani said that the articles were brought from outside and Officer-in-charge (informant PW 1) uttered to shut his mouth. The evidence is produced below, word for word:

জব্দ তালিকা লিখার সময় ডাঃ গণি সাহেবের সাথে পুলিশের তর্কাতর্কি হয় এবং ডাক্তার সাহেব বলেন যে, ঐ মালামাল বাহির হইতে আনা হয়।

উপস্থিত ডাঃ গণি বলিয়াছিল যে, জব্দকৃত মালামাল বাহির হইতে আনা হইয়াছে এবং তাহা নিয়া এস,পি,র সাথে তর্কাতর্কি হয়। এ সময় ওসি আঃ সালাম ডাঃ গণিকে বলে  stop your mouth.

By evidence of PW 5 who is no other than a public seizure list witness the prosecution case that incriminating articles i.e. materials for preparation of bombs and cocktails, had been found and recovered from occurrence building stood flung to the wind.

47. PW 6, though another seizure list witness, made disclosure that he found the dead bodies of two persons and found empty pots of sweet pilau coloured with saffron (Jorda), window rod and broken pieces of glasses lying scattered and put his signature in seizure list but the fact remains that PW 6 approached on the scene building on the following day of incident. Police took control of the occurrence building and the premises on 15-3-1999 and it was not possible on the part of PW 6 to enter into the incident building. Moreover, statement of PW 6 was recorded under section 161 of the Code after a period of 52 days of the incident. His evidence is to be left out of consideration in view of consistent judicial pronouncements in good number of cases such as Paran Chandra Baroi vs State 1982 BCR 292, Nurul Huq and others vs State 1982 BCR 332, State vs Moqbul Hossain 1986 BLD 34 = 37 DLR 156, Muslimuddin and others vs State 1987 BLD (AD) 1 = 38 DLR (AD) 311 and Sharafat Mondal and others vs State 2005 BCR 392 = 11 BLC 1 (wherein one of us, AK Badrul Huq, J, was a party).

48. True it is that PWs 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15, 17, 20, 21, 22, 23, 30 and 31 had been declared hostile as they had given a total go-by to prosecution case and lent assurance to the defence case but the evidence of above PWs did not get washed away as because they were declared hostile. In Md Shah Alam and others vs State 1985 BLD (AD) 198 Chowdhury ATM Masud J speaking for the Court held, that a witness even if declared hostile can be relied upon if considering his entire evidence including the cross-examination by the parties, the Court is satisfied about the credibility of the witness. In Siddique Munshi vs State 44 DLR AD 169 it has been stated: Witness is not necessarily hostile if he reveals the truth. Established practice now forming a rule of law, regarding the evidence of a hostile witness is that the whole of his evidence so far as it affects both the parties, favourably or unfavorably, must be considered and the Court which gets the opportunity to observe his demeanor is at liberty to make assessment of the evidence. If corroboration from other sources is available to the evidence of a hostile witness there is no reason why his evidence should be rejected outright. In State of Uttar Pradesh vs Chat Ram AIR 1985 (SC) 1543 = 1989 SCC (Cri) 388 = (1989) 2 SCC 425 Supreme Court of India observed that merely because a witness is declared hostile his entire evidence does not get excluded or rendered unworthy of credit.

<u>49. Druta Bichar Tribunal, in characterizing convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik guilty found that through evidence and defence case it had been established that in bed-room of his house cocktail had been prepared and bomb or cocktail exploded and explosive substances, cocktails and elements for preparation of cocktail had been found from the house under his control and it had been, also, established that he provided the accused persons his house for the purpose of preparing cocktail and others by explosive substances and, thus, aided in the preparation of bombs. The above finding reached by Druta Bichar Tribunal is absolutely against evidence and materials on record and the said finding perilously borders on perversity.</u>

50. In Bimal Pershad Jain vs Emperor (Supra) referred to from the side of convict-appellants Baboo Ram Gupta was tried under section 6 of Explosive Substances Act of 1908 and he was convicted under the above section. Baboo Ram Gupta was alleged to have supplied materials for manufacturing explosive substances with the knowledge that explosive substances were to be manufactured with intent to endanger life or cause serious injury to the property in British India. Jai Lal, J held:

Section 6—Explosive Substances Act of 1908, provides that any person who, inter alia, by the supply of materials procures, counsels, aids, abets or is accessory to the commission of any offence, shall be punished with the punishment provided for the offence. I take it that the intention to procure, counsel, aid, abet or to be accessory to the commission of offence is a necessary ingredient of the offence under section 6 of The Act and ordinarily it is the primary intention of the accused that must be taken into consideration in determining his guilt. Taking into consideration all circumstances, I am of the opinion Baboo Ram Gupta cannot be convicted of an offence under section 6, Explosive Substances Act of 1908, even assuming that he personally arranged with Kailash Patti and others for the supply of chemicals and at that time he suspected that they might be used for illegal purposes.

Baboo Ram Gupta was acquitted of the charge.

51. In Abdul Rahim vs King (Supra), also, relied upon from the side of convict-appellant, Noor Mohammad, Jainul and Abdul Rahim were found guilty under section 6 of Explosive Substances Act. The only fact established by the prosecution against Abdul Rahim was that he and his brother Noor Mohammad occupied a room in the house in which room marks of blood were found following explosion of a bomb. There had been no evidence that Abdul Rahim either procured, counselled, aided or abetted the commission of the offence nor there was any evidence that Abdul Rahim either supplied the money or solicited for money or provided the premises or supplied the materials for commission of any offence under the Explosive Substances Act. In pronouncing a Judgment of acquittal upon Abdul Rahim it has been held that mere presence of accused, in a room along with his brother who was found guilty under The Act does not make him guilty under section 6 and failure to disclose what happened in room did not make accused an accessory.

These two Judicial authorities are of significant assistance to the convict-appellants.

52. This drives us to the framing of charge against convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik. Charge has been framed in the following language:

“আপনার বিরুদ্ধে অভিযোগ এই যে, বিগত ১৫-৩-১৯৯৯ ইং সময় অনুমান ১৫-৪০ ঘটিকা ও ২৪-৩-১৯৯৯ ইং সময় অনুমান ১৫-৪০ ঘটিকা ও ২৪-৩-১৯৯৯ ইং সময় অনুমান ৮-০০ ঘটিকা হইতে ১৪-৩০ ঘটিকা সুনামগঞ্জ জেলার ছাতক থানা ও পৌরসভাধীন ২০০ উদয়াচল মন্ডলীভোগ হাসপাতাল রোডস্থিত আপনার মালিকানাধীন বাসভবনের দ্বিতলে পশ্চিম দিক হইতে ৩ নং কক্ষে আসামী গোপাল চন্দ্র দাস গং মোট ৭ জন আসামী আপনার সহিত গোপন যোগাযোগীতে থাকিয়া পূর্বাক্রোশে ও পূর্ব পরিকল্পিতভাবে অন্যের জীবন, ব্যক্তি বা সম্পত্তি বিপন্ন করিয়া ছাতক শহরে আপনাকে রাজনৈতিকভাবে প্রতিষ্ঠিত করার লক্ষ্যে আপনার সম্পত্তিতে ও আপনার স্বার্থে ও অর্থে বেআইনী ভাবে ও বিদ্বেষ প্রসূত ভাবে বিষ্ফোরক দ্রব্যাদি সংগ্রহ করিয়া তাহা নিজ দখলে ও নিয়ন্ত্রনে রাখিয়া ককটেল বোমা প্রস্তুত করাকালীন সময়ে অসাবধানতা বশতঃ এক মারাত্নক বিষ্ফোরন ঘটে যাহাতে আসামী আবুল কালাম বাবুল ও আরিফ হায়দার ঘটনাস্থলে নিহত হয় এবং আসামী আবু লেইছ চৌধুরী মারাত্নকভাবে জখম প্রাপ্ত হন ও উক্ত বিষ্ফোরনে আপনার উক্ত বসত গৃহের দ্বিতলের ঘটনাস্থল রুমের দেয়াল ইত্যাদির মারাত্নক ক্ষতি সাধিত হইয়াছে এবং উক্ত ঘটনার পর বিগত ২৪-৩-১৯৯৯ ইং তারিখে আপনার উক্ত বাসভবনের দ্বিতলের ৫ নং কক্ষ হইতে আসামী গোপাল চন্দ্র দাস গংদের প্রস্তুতকৃত ১০ টি Home made তাজা ককটেল ও আরও অন্যান্য বিষ্ফোরক দ্রব্যাদি বাংলাদেশ সেনাবাহিনীর বিশেষজ্ঞ দল কর্তৃক আসামী গোপাল চন্দ্র দাস গংদের হেফাজতে ও সংরক্ষণে থাকাবস্থায় উদ্ধার করা হইয়াছে। আসামী গোপাল চন্দ্র দাস গংদের হেফাজতে ও সংরক্ষনে থাকাবস্থায় উদ্ধার করা হইয়াছে। আসামী গোপাল চন্দ্র গং আপনার খুবই ঘনিষ্ঠ বিশ্বস্থ ও আপনজন বিধায় তাহারা আপনার বাসভবনকে নিরাপদ স্থান মনে করিয়া আপনার অনুরোধে ও সম্মতিতে বিষ্ফোরক দ্রব্যাদি সংগ্রহ করিয়া উক্ত ঘটনা সংগঠিত করিয়াছে। উক্ত কার্য্য করিয়া আপনি বিষ্ফোরক উপাদানাবলী আইন ১৯০৮ সনের ৬ নং ধারা মোতাবেক শাস্তিযোগ্য অপরাধ সংগঠন করিয়াছেন যাহা অত্রাদালত কর্তৃক বিচার্য্য।

<u>53. To back up charge no evidence had been led that on 15-3-1999 convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik in furtive league with accused Gopal Chandra Das and six (6) others, with intent to endanger life or property of other persons and to establish himself politically, out of his own interest and fund, procured explosive substances and kept those in his possession and control in room No. 3 of the two-storied building and also, in room No. 5 of the building. Prosecution signally failed to validate charge through legal evidence.</u>

54. From evidences, materials on record and fact and circumstances of the case, the irresistible conclusion which can be drawn is that prosecution manifestly failed to drive home the offence of section 6 of the Explosive Substances Act against convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik and a judgment of acquittal was required to be showered upon him. Druta Bichar Tribunal was not at all justified in awarding conviction upon him on finding him guilty of offence of section 6 of The Act of 1908.

55. This leads us to the destiny of convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury.

56. Convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury, stood convicted for offence of section 4 of The Explosive Substances Act. Druta Bichar Tribunal did not specifically state whether he was convicted under section 4(a) or 4(b) of The Act. In the face of positive decision arrived at by Druta Bichar Tribunal that convict-appellant and co-convict Gopal Chandra Das with intent to endanger life or cause serious injury to property kept different articles and materials for manufacturing bombs/cocktails under their possession and control, conviction prized upon convict-appellant was squarely under section 4(b) of The Act. Offence of section 4(a) of The Act was not pressed into service against the convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury.

57. Section 4(b) of The Act provides that any person who makes or has in his possession or under his control any explosive substance with intent by means thereof to endanger life, or cause serious injury to person or property in Bangladesh or to enable any other person by means thereof to endanger life or cause serious injury to person or property in Bangladesh; shall, whether any explosion does or does not take place and whether any injury to person or property has been actually caused or not, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to twenty years, and shall not be less than three years.

58. "Explosive substance" has been defined in section 2 of The Act Section 2 postulates that the expression "explosive substance" shall be deemed to include any materials for making any explosive substance; also any apparatus, machine implement or material used, or intended to be used, or adapted for causing or aiding in causing, any explosion in or with any explosive substance; also any part of any such apparatus, machine or implement.

59. The words "possession and control" appear in section 4(b) of the Act of 1908. Pollock and Wright in the book on "Possession in the Common Law" state that in common parlance a man is said to possess anything of which he has apparent control or from use of which he has the apparent power of excluding others.

60. Salmond in his Book on "Jurisprudence" expressed the opinion that test for determining whether a person is in possession of anything is, whether he is in general control of it.

61. "Possession" is expressed in Corpus Juris Secondum, 72 qs 233 in the following terms: "The closest relation of facts which can exist between a corporeal thing and the person who possesses it implying an actual physical contact, as by sitting or standing upon a thing denoting custody coupled with a right of interest of proprietorship and possession is inclusive of "custody" although "custody" is not tantamount to "possession".

62. The concept of possession under the Penal Law or any other law is not necessarily the same as the concept of "possession" under the Act of 1908 or The Arms Act, 1878. Concept of "possession" under The Act of 1908 or The Act of 1878 connotes an element of consciousness in the person charged with the offence.

63. Possession as a test or an element of crime must be of such character as can relate to the fundamental principle of "menses" in Criminal Jurisprudence. The animus must be there and the "menses" must, also, be there. The animus is the very basis of any legal concept of possession. Wherever possession is a basis of crime, "consciousness" or 'animus' must be established. It is, thus, the element of "intention" or "consciousness" or "knowledge" which must be established and must be present as a fact before possession under the Explosive Substances Act can be said to constitute an offence.

64. Control in section 4(b) means that the accused must have such power over explosive substances that he can direct its custody production, use or disposal in some manner. "Control" in context means power or ability to regulate the keeping or possession or use to endanger life and cause serious injury to a person or property

65. Possession or control essential to constitute an offence under section 4(b), thus, must be "conscious possession" and "effective control" over explosive substances to endanger life or to cause serious injury to person or property.

66. Some Judicial pronouncements of Superior Courts on possession and control under the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 and the Arms Act of 1878 may be taken stock of.

67. In Kuldip Chand vs Emperor, AIR 1934 Lahore 718 relied upon from the side of convict-appellant, it has been laid down: Possession must be conscious and intelligent possession and not merely the physical presence of the accused in proximity or even in close proximity of the offending object. These are the important elements which go to make up an offence under section 4(b) of the Act.

68. In The State of Bihar vs Amir Hasan (Supra) referred to from the side of convict-appellants it has been stated:

"Possession" under section 5 means conscious possession but it need not always be manual possession, that is, possession by physically touching the incriminating object. 'Control' is a somewhat wide concept than 'possession' but there again the control must be actual control and not merely constructive or notional control.

69. In Mohamad Usman Mohammad Hussain Maniyar and another vs The State of Maharashtra (Supra) placed from the side of convict-appellant, the observation of the Supreme Court of India is couched in the following terms:

In order to bring home the offence under section 5 the prosecution has to prove (i) that the substance in question is explosive substance; (ii) that the accused makes or knowingly has in his possession or under his control any explosive substance; and (iii) that he does so under such circumstances as to give rise to a reasonable suspicion that he is not doing so for a lawful object.

70. In Arshadullah vs State 21 DLR 684 it has been said:

The word possession means exclusive possession and the word control means effective control:

71. In Kashem alias Md Abul Kashem vs State 47 DLR 438. Gain Chand vs Emperor AIR 1933 (Lah ) 315, Emperor vs Santa Singh AIR 1944 (Lah) 339 and Arshadullah vs State 21 DLR 684 had been taken into consideration and it has been held—

To constitute offences under section 19(f) of the Arms Act, 1878 and section 5 of Explosive Substances Act of 1908. Possession and control under section 19(f) of the Arms Act and section 5 of Explosive Substances Act must mean conscious possession and actual control with necessary mens rea.

72. In Amritalal Hazra and others vs Emperor (Supra). Import of section 4(b) of the Act of 1908 had been ruminated. A good number of Judicial decisions had been taken into account to bear witness to under what circumstances a person may be deemed to be in possession of an explosive substance. A Division Bench consisting of Mookerjee and Richardson, JJ held:

No useful purpose would be served by an analysis of the circumstances of the various cases discussed at the Bar. It is sufficient to say that while it is not necessary to prove manual possession of the explosive substance by the accused, it must be proved that it was in his power or control; possession to be punishable must also be possession with knowledge and assent.

73. In Kanta Proshad vs State AIR 1961 Allahabad 438 on taking, into account more than 50 cases on all aspects of possession. Allahabad High Court reached the following conclusion:

Corpus and animus are only conditions of acquisition of possession and are not possession itself and that possession once acquired may continue even though either or both disappear and that no single theory will explain possession, that corpus and animus have no fixed meaning but are facts which the law generally requires for the commencement of possession and that possession carries with it the right to possess.

74. In Norendra Nath Mozumdar vs State AIR 1951 Calcutta 140 it has been laid down:

It is the element of intention or consciousness or knowledge, which must be established and must be present as a fact before possession under the Arms Act can be said to constitute an offence. It has been further held: Control in section 19(f) means that the accused must have such power over the weapon that he can direct its custody, production, use or disposal in some manner.

75. In Babul vs State 57 DLR 158 (wherein one of us AK Badrul Huq was author Judge) it has been held:

"Possession" or "Control" essential to constitute offence under section 19(f) of the Arms Act must be conscious possession or actual control and possession or control of incriminating articles constitutes offence. To constitute offence there must be mens rea or guilty knowledge. Existence of mens rea or guilty knowledge is the sine qua non for offence of possessing weapon of crime.

76. In the unreported case of Md Yusuf and others vs State Criminal Appeal No. 3979 of 2003 (Judicial verdict pronounced by us) it has been stated:

Concept of possession under the Penal Law or any other law is not necessarily the same as the concept of "possession" under the Explosive Substances Act of 1908 or the Arms Act, 1878. Concept of possession under the Explosive Substances Act of 1908 or the Arms Act of 1878 connotes an element of consciousness in the person charged with the offence.

Further observation is:

"Possession" or "Control" essential to constitute offence under section 4(b) of the Act of 1908, thus, must be conscious possession or control of explosive substance to endanger life or cause serious injury to person or property.

77. Lutfar Rahman alias Arju and another vs State 51 DLR (AD) 120 cited from the side of respondent-State is a case under section 19A and 19(f) of the Arms Act. In the said case Mukim Gazi was apprehended and one revolver and some cartridges were recovered from him. No arms were recovered from other accused persons. It was held that the revolver and cartridges recovered from Mukim Gazi were only in his exclusive possession and law will ascribe joint possession in such circumstances. In the ease in hand nothing had been recovered nor seized from convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury.

78. In the above discussed cases, fact and circumstances might be different but the crystallized views emanated from the above Judicial authorities is that element of intention or conscious possession or knowledge and, also, effective control in custody, production, use or disposal in any manner must be present in driving home the offence punishable under section 4(b) of the Explosive Substances Act of 1908 to an accused person charged under the above section.

79. Admittedly, convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury used to stay in the occurrence building. He was injured by explosion of bombs/cocktails. PW 26 Dr Mrinal Kumar Das examined him medically. Of course, no certificate had been issued by him. It came to light from the second information report and, also, from version furnished by Informant PW 1 that explosion occurred in room No. 3 of the first floor of the occurrence building and Abul Kalam Babul and Arif Haider died and convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury sustained injury. No evidence came forth that the convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury had been in room No.3 of occurrence building. It has been stated in the foregoing paragraph that the evidence of PW 5 knocked the bottom out of the prosecution case that incriminating articles for manufacturing bombs had been recovered and seized from occurrence building and it has, also, been further manifested from the testimony of PW 5 that Dr Abdul Gani sup-plied information that articles (incriminating) had been brought from outside and there had been war of words between Dr Abdul Gani and Officer (Informant PW 1) told Dr Abdul Gani to shut his mouth.

80. Index of sketch map No. 2 (Exhibit 17) manifests that "C" was shown  the occurrence room where explosion took place and accused Belal, cousin brother of convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik, was stated to have stayed there. "D" was shown as the room of convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury and from that room cocktail contained in a pot of Elite Paint colour, Ramdao and Rimball and Empty was stated to have been recovered Prosecution's positive case was that explosion occurred in the room of convict-appellant Muhibur Rahman Manik. Index (Exhibit 17) demonstratively falsified the prosecution version. Admittedly no explosion happened in the room of Abu Lyes Choudhury which was shown as "D" in Index (Exhibit 17). No evidence came forth evidencing that the room "D" as shown in Index was in exclusive possession of convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury. There is nothing on record that convict-appellant had conscious possession or control over the articles or he had guilty mind to commit any offence to endanger life and cause serious injury to person or property. Moreover, Exhibit 3 is seizure list prepared on 16-3-1999 and Exhibit 6 is the photocopy of seizure list dated 16-3-1399. Exhibit 7 is seizure list dated 19-5-1999. Exhibits 3 and 6 do not indicate that articles such as cocktail contained in Elite Paint color pot, Ramdao and 0.22 Rimballs and Empty noted in Index allegedly recovered from the room which was shown as "D" in Index and was stated to be the room of convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury were at all seized under seizure list.

81. Recovery and seizure of the articles from the room shown as "D" in Index and was stated to be the room of convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury stood totally demolished and the question of possession and control on the part of convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury, also, did not and does not arise at all.

<u>82. True it is that convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury suffered injury. Sufferance of injuries cannot be an inference that explosive substance had been under his possession or control and he along with deceased Abul Kalam Babul and Arif Haider were manufacturing bombs/cocktails. Any conclusion that the accused is guilty under section 4(b) would be a mere conjecture, speculation or guess which are not in law and justice permissible grounds to base a verdict of conviction and sentence upon convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury.</u>

<u>83. On evidence and materials before us, we hold that there is no iota of evidence from which any legitimate inference of possession can be drawn against convict-appellant Abu Lyes Choudhury.</u>

84. Druta Bichar Tribunal misdirected itself in its approach of the case and in resolving the controversy. It committed a serious error in presuming the guilt of convict-appellants and trying, thereafter, to find out the other reason to justify such a conclusion without an objective, independent and impartial analysis or assessment of evidences and materials brought on record before recording a finding of guilt upon convict-appellants. Inherent infirmities which were blatant and perceptible in the prosecution anecdote had been glossed over. Judgment of conviction and sentence does not appear to carry marks of true dispensation of justice, rather transpires to be a sheer travesty of justice. Judgment of conviction and sentence cannot have any backing by this Court.

85. On bestowing our dispassionate consideration to all the pros and cons of the prosecution version and browsing fact and circumstances of the case, we can safely come to the conclusion that prosecution failed to establish its case against the convict-appellants beyond any silhouette of doubt. Evidence produced by prosecution and materials relied upon to fasten the guilt upon convict-appellants only points needle of suspicion and doubt towards them. Standard required to be achieved by prosecuting agency to demand conviction is very much wanting. Boon of doubt, thus, can conveniently be showered upon convict-appellants and a verdict of acquittal is required to be passed upon them.

86. Points formulated stand answered in the following epithet :

i. Prosecution could not succeed in bringing home the charge to the doors of convict-appellants beyond any pale of doubt.

ii. Verdict of conviction and sentence awarded upon convict-appellants cannot be sustained in law, evidences, materials brought on record and fact and circumstances of the case and, also, in safe dispensation of Criminal Justice.

iii. Convict-appellants can be emancipated of the charge staged against them on bestowing a ruling of acquittal on finding them not guilty of the charge.

87. In the premises of the discourse made above and reasons counted the inevitable conclusion which flows is,

Criminal Appeal No. 3653 of 2004 presented by convict-appellants Muhibur Rahman Manik, son of Haji Kalandar Ali and Abu Lyes Choudhury, son of Abu Taher Chowdhury is allowed. Judgment of conviction and sentence recorded on 9-10-2004 by Druta Bichar Tribunal, Sylhet in Druta Bichar Tribunal Case No. 4 of 2003 in respect of convict-appellants stands set aside. Convict-appellants are not found guilty of offence of sections 6 and 4 respectively of the Explosive Substances Act, 1908 and they are liberated of the charge staged against them and are acquitted thereof. They are set at liberty at once if not required in connection with any other case.

Lower Court Records be sent down at once.

End.
